previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, migraines, sleep apnea, and recent chest pain evaluation was admitted for acute lower back pain that began a week prior without trauma. The pain was localized to the lower back and buttocks, with no radiation, weakness, or bowel/bladder changes. She had been seen in the ED previously and underwent an MRI that revealed a herniated disc at L5-S1 with possible impingement on the right S1 nerve root. She was admitted for pain management and further care. During her stay, she received oral hydromorphone and acetaminophen for pain, started on a six-day steroid taper, and prescribed tizanidine for muscle relaxation. A back brace was recommended, and home physical therapy was arranged. Her diabetes and hypertension were managed with continued outpatient medications, and she was treated for opioid-induced constipation with Miralax and Colace. She improved clinically and was discharged home in good condition with follow-up planned with spine specialists and clear instructions on warning signs requiring urgent care.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ y.o. woman w/ pmh migraines, pseudotumor 
cerebri who presented with headache and LLQ pain. 
   
#. Headache - The headache was secondary to HTN, migraine, or 
pseudotumor cerebri, as the patient has a h/o these conditions. 
The LP showed no evidence of infection. CT head was reported as 
a normal study. Neuro recommended that the patient be restarted 
on Topamax and Diamox for her headache, and to follow-up with 
Dr. ___ as an outpatient. The patient's pain 
improved over the course of her hospitalization and was switched 
from IV morphine to PO oxycodone. Although the headache 
resolved, the patient had persistent nausea and vomiting. The 
patient was given IVF, zofran, and reglan with some relief. 
    
#. Abdominal pain - The patient had severe LLQ abdominal pain 
when she was in the emergency department during an LP. CT 
abdomen/pelvis showed no evidence of abnormalities. There was no 
elevation in WBC or abnormal UA, so UTI was unlikely. The LLQ 
abdominal pain resolved without intervention.
   
#. Increased LFTs - The patient was found to have elevated 
AST/ALT (53/67). The most likely etiology was overuse of 
acetominophen. The patient was found to be taking Percocet 1 tab 
q6h and Tylenol 1g q6h at home. She was counseled about 
appropriate use of medications with acetominophen, and no pain 
medications with acetominophen were given during this 
hospitalization. The LFTs improved to WNL during her stay.
     
#. Hypertension - The patient arrived with BP 197/122 and was 
given a dose of Labetolol. Her BP ran low (~100/60) during much 
of the rest of her hospitalization. Many of her BP medications 
were held, as her baseline SBP is typicaly ~160. She was 
discharged with instructions to continue taking Lisinopril and 
Clonidine, reduce Labetalol dose from 200mg TID to ___ BID, 
and to hold spironolactone, amlodipine, and HCTZ; if her 
SBP>160, we recommended that she take her previous doses of BP 
medications. She was scheduled an appointment with her PCP ___. 
___ on ___ to follow-up regarding her BP regimen.

Discharge Instructions:
You were treated in the hospital for severe headache. We started 
you on intravenous morphine and switched you to oral oxycodone 
for pain control. We also treated you for nausea and gave you 
intravenous fluids. 
    
Your blood tests showed some elevated liver function tests. We 
believe this is because you were taking Percocet 1 tab every 6 
hours and Tylenol 1g every 6 hours for pain when you were at 
home. Percocet and Tylenol both contain Acetopminophen, which 
can be harmful to your liver when you take too much. You can 
continue to take the same dose of Percocet at home, but please 
decrease your Tyelonol dose to 500mg every 6 hours; or you can 
take Tylenol 1g every 6 hours INSTEAD of the Percocet. Do not 
exceed 4g Acetominophen in 1 day!
     
Your blood pressure during your hospitalization was much lower 
than your reported baseline of systolic blood pressure in the 
160s. We held some of your blood pressure medications while you 
were here. Please monitor your blood pressure closely when you 
get home. We recommend the following changes to your blood 
pressure regimen for today:
1. Continue to take Lisinopril and Clonidine as prescribed
2. Reduce your Labetalol dose from 200mg three times a day to 
100mg twice a day.
3. Do not take Spironolactone, Amlodipine, or 
Hydrochlorothiazide for now.
If your blood pressure is >160, please take your previous doses 
of Labetalol and Spironolactone. 
You have an appointment with your primary care physician, ___. 
___ at 10:15am. Please discuss your 
blood pressure and medications with him at the appointment. 
  
You were started on the following medications to treat and help 
prevent return of your headache:
1. Topiramate 25mg twice a day
2. Acetazolamide (Diamox) 250mg twice a day
Please follow-up with your primary care physician and 
neurologist regarding these new medications.
   
You also had nausea while you were here in the hospital. You 
will be discharged on Reglan to help control your nausea.
     
If you experience worsening headache, changes in vision, 
dizziness, fevers, chills, chest pain, or any other concerning 
symptoms, please call your primary care physician or return to 
the emergency department.
    
It was a pleasure meeting you and participating in your care.
